title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 19: Equatorial Reality v. Mayfair Theater: General Principles Do Not Decide Specific Cases
keywords: Equatorial Realty Development v. Mayfair Theater
General propositions do not decide specific cases
Non nudis pactis sed traditione dominia rerum transferantur
primary_topics: Chapter 19 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's account of his ponencia in Equatorial Realty Development v. Mayfair Theater, built on the Holmes-derived thesis that 'General propositions do not decide specific cases' and that each case 'has its own flesh and blood' and cannot be ruled upon on 'isolated clinical classroom principles.'

The civil-law holding that ownership passes not by agreement but by tradition or delivery, so Equatorial -- never having been placed in actual control and possession because of Mayfair's timely objection -- never became owner and was therefore never entitled to the civil fruits of the property.

The refusal to let the abstract rule that 'a rescissible contract is valid until rescinded' decide the concrete question of rentals, and the parallel holding that Equatorial's bad faith, already settled and final in the 1996 mother case, independently barred any award to it.

The 10-5 split within the Court, reproduced at length: Justice Melo's concurrence that granting the petition would 'reward bad faith,' Justice Vitug's dissent classifying rescissible contracts as valid and effective until rescinded, and Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's dissent arguing that ownership and possession had in fact passed to Equatorial.
sub_topics: CJP opens by quoting the preface of his own Decision, paraphrasing Justice Oliver Wendeel Holmes Jr.: general propositions do not decide specific cases; laws are interpreted 'in the context of the peculiar factual situation of each proceeding.'

He states the petitioner's theory -- that a rescissible contract of sale is valid until actually rescinded, so the buyer could collect rentals in the interim -- and concedes it would have been 'theoretically correct' but for the absence of delivery.

The facts: Carmelo & Bauermann leased land and two buildings to Mayfair Theater for 20 years under contracts granting Mayfair a right of first refusal, then sold the properties to Equatorial for P11,300,000 without first offering them to Mayfair.

The 1996 mother case (GR No. 106063) rescinded that sale and ordered Carmelo to return the price and let Mayfair buy at P11,300,000; execution stalled because Carmelo could no longer be located, so Mayfair deposited the money with the Manila Clerk of Court and stayed on the premises.

After the leases expired, Equatorial sued to collect rentals; the trial court dismissed the claim and wrongly called the Deed of Sale 'void at its inception,' and Equatorial elevated the rental claim to the Supreme Court.

By a vote of 10 to 5, in a ponencia CJP 'had the honor of writing,' the Court held that 'no right of ownership was transferred from Carmelo to Equatorial in view of a patent failure to deliver the property to the buyer.'

The basic parameters of the law on sales: rent is a civil fruit belonging to the owner by right of accession; ownership is a real right acquired only upon delivery, 'not by contract alone, but by tradition or delivery' -- Non nudis pactis sed traditione dominia rerum transferantur.

Delivery is 'a composite act, a thing in which both parties must join and the minds of both parties concur,' and both actual and constructive delivery require the vendor's absolute giving up of control and the vendee's assumption of it.

Applied to the facts: execution of a public instrument is only a legal fiction of delivery that holds 'only when there is no impediment'; Mayfair's court action impugning the sale was 'a legally sufficient impediment,' so 'fiction yields to reality - the delivery has not been effected.'

Article 1164 is answered by Article 1385: rescission obliges the return of the things sold 'together with their fruits, and the price with its interest,' so rentals paid would have had to be returned anyway.

CJP confronts the awkward record -- the mother case, Justice Padilla's Separate Opinion and even his own Separate Concurring Opinion all said Equatorial received rentals -- and answers that these do not concede actual delivery.

The explanation: Equatorial had filed two ejectment suits (Civil Case No. 121570 in 1987 and Civil Case No. 131944 in 1990) which Mayfair won; Mayfair paid rentals only to keep physical possession under the Rules of Court, 'merely to avoid imminent eviction,' not in recognition of Equatorial's title.

The bottom line: a rescissible contract may theoretically be valid until rescinded, but that general principle 'is not decisive'; what is decisive is that ownership is acquired by tradition, and the sale 'was judicially rescinded before it could be consummated.'

A second, independent ground -- bad faith: the mother case, final and executory, found Equatorial a buyer in bad faith whose lawyers had studied the lease contracts, so it is entitled 'solely to the return of the purchase price it paid to Carmelo; no more, no less.'

Since the mother case had categorically denied interest, 'another fruit of ownership,' rentals cannot be granted 'without mocking this Court's en banc Decision'; if petitioner suffered loss it 'must bear it in silence,' else 'bad faith would be rewarded instead of punished.'

The Melo concurrence: the issue was already squarely resolved in 1996; petitioner's submissions are 'deceiving'; granting the petition would reward bad faith after 23 years of deprivation and the 'fantastic and groundless' claim of P115,947,867.00 -- and Mayfair, were it a natural person, could have asked for moral damages.

The Vitug dissent: rescissible contracts are the least infirm of defective contracts, 'valid, binding and effective until rescinded'; rescission under Article 1381 is prospective and unlike resolution under Article 1191, so ownership passed to Equatorial from July 30, 1978 until finality on March 17, 1997, and 'ownership... is never described as being either in good faith or in bad faith.'

The Sandoval-Gutierrez dissent: the mother case ordered Equatorial to execute deeds 'to return ownership to Carmelo,' which presupposes transfer; receiving rentals is an exercise of possession through another; Mayfair as lessee held only as a mere holder and so was no impediment; and under Guzman v. Court of Appeals and Article 1658 the lessee owed rent to the new owner.

stances.claim: Equatorial never acquired ownership of the property, because ownership is transferred not by contract alone but by tradition or delivery, and Mayfair's timely objection was a legally sufficient impediment that prevented delivery from taking place.

notable_anecdotes: CJP notes he prefaced his own Decision by paraphrasing Justice Oliver Wendeel Holmes Jr., and then repeats the same line at the end of the chapter as the case's lesson.
He interrupts his own doctrinal opening -- 'But this is getting ahead of the story. Let me first state the facts' -- before narrating the Carmelo-Mayfair-Equatorial sale.

He recounts that the 1996 Decision could not be executed because Carmelo 'could no longer be located,' leaving Mayfair to deposit P11,300,000 with the Manila Clerk of Court while staying on the premises.

He discloses the uncomfortable fact that his own Separate Concurring Opinion in the mother case had itself recognized that Equatorial received rentals, and then explains why that does not concede delivery.

He reports Justice Melo's arithmetic of injury -- 23 years of deprivation and a claim of P115,947,867.00 -- and Melo's observation that Mayfair, were it a natural person, could have asked for moral damages instead.
He records that the case had originally been assigned for study and report to Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez, who ended up writing a dissent against the ponencia he wrote.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' recounts Panganiban's ponencia in Equatorial Realty Development v. Mayfair Theater, which he prefaced by paraphrasing Justice Oliver Wendeel Holmes Jr.: 'General propositions do not decide specific cases,' since laws are read in the peculiar factual situation of each proceeding and each case 'has its own flesh and blood.' Carmelo & Bauermann had leased land and two buildings to Mayfair for twenty years under contracts giving Mayfair a right of first refusal, then sold the properties to Equatorial for P11,300,000 without offering them to Mayfair; in the 1996 'mother case' (GR No. 106063) the Court rescinded that sale, but execution stalled because Carmelo could not be found, so Mayfair deposited the price and stayed on. When Equatorial later sued for rentals, arguing that a rescissible contract is valid until actually rescinded, the Court held by 10-5 that 'no right of ownership was transferred from Carmelo to Equatorial in view of a patent failure to deliver the property to the buyer.' Panganiban laid down the basic parameters -- rent is a civil fruit of ownership, and ownership is a real right transferred 'not by contract alone, but by tradition or delivery' -- and reasoned that execution of a public instrument is only a legal fiction of delivery that holds when no impediment exists; Mayfair's timely court objection was such an impediment, so 'fiction yields to reality.' He explained that Mayfair's rental payments, made while two ejectment suits were pending, were 'paid merely to avoid imminent eviction' and conceded nothing. As an independent ground he invoked the final finding of Equatorial's bad faith: it is entitled 'solely to the return of the purchase price... no more, no less,' and must bear its loss 'in silence,' lest 'bad faith would be rewarded instead of punished.' He then reproduced Justice Melo's concurrence, Justice Vitug's dissent on the nature of rescissible contracts, and Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's dissent arguing that ownership and possession had in fact passed.
